subject: physics
title: ZIMSEC O-Level Physics

officialDocument.title: O Level Physics Syllabus, Forms 3 - 4, 2015 - 2022 (Ministry of Primary and Secondary Education, Curriculum Development and Technical Services), examined by ZIMSEC at O Level
officialDocument.publisher: Ministry of Primary and Secondary Education (Curriculum Development and Technical Services) / Zimbabwe School Examinations Council (ZIMSEC)

sourceNote: Topic and subtopic headings and numbers are transcribed from the Ministry's O Level Physics Syllabus Forms 3 - 4 (2015 - 2022): topics from '6.0 Topics', subtopics from the scope and sequence chart and the '8.0 Competency matrix', each with its Form. Learning-objective statements are our own paraphrase of the competency matrix; their codes (subtopic number + running number, or a word prefix for unnumbered nodes) are ours, not the board's.
notes: Source status (checked 2026-10-08): the Ministry document 'O- Level Physics Syllabus Forms 3 - 4, 2015 - 2022' (Curriculum Development and Technical Services, 2015) was read from a third-party text rendering at https://www.readkong.com/page/o-level-physics-syllabus-forms-3-4-2015-2022-2524754, which is not an official Ministry or ZIMSEC address. The preamble, aims, objectives, topic list, the whole scope and sequence chart and the competency matrix up to 14.4 Electronic components were read. The rest of the document (the remaining electronics and the atomic and nuclear physics matrix pages, and section 9.0 Assessment) was not available. A copy at revision.co.zw could not be opened (its TLS certificate does not match the host). Verify every heading against an official copy and replace the officialDocument URL once one is confirmed.

Not recorded because the assessment section was not read: the subject code (commonly cited as 4023, not printed in the pages read), the papers and their durations, marks and weightings, and calculator rules. No components are listed and no mock exams are built for this syllabus until they are confirmed.

Electronics numbering: the competency matrix numbers 14.1 Thermionic emission, 14.2 Diodes, 14.3 Rectification and 14.4 Electronic components; the scope and sequence chart lists 14.1 Electronic components and 14.2 Logic gates. The matrix numbering is used, and Logic gates (from the chart: circuit symbols and truth tables) is an unnumbered node.

Topic 15 (atomic model; isotopes; radioactivity: definition, types of emission and their characteristics, use, storage, handling and impact) comes from the scope and sequence chart only. Background radiation and detection, decay equations, half-life and nuclear fission and fusion are not mentioned there, so those concepts are not mapped to this syllabus; add them if the competency matrix includes them.
The competency matrix numbers 'Social and economic considerations of using fuels' 8.1, like the four-stroke engine; it is kept as an unnumbered second subtopic of topic 8.

ZIMSEC-only content mapped here (not in Cambridge IGCSE 0625): the equations of motion (2.1), atmospheric pressure, barometers, manometers and hydraulics (3.6), simple machines (4), mechanical structures (5), thermometers and specific latent heat (7.2), Charles's law and the equation of state (7.1), the four-stroke engine and fuels (8), primary and secondary cells (11.2), R = ρl/A (11.3), magnetising and demagnetising (12.1), thermionic emission, rectification, electronic components and logic gates (14). The 3.2 note says conservation of momentum is not required, so only p = mv content applies to ZIMSEC.

Curriculum change: the Heritage-Based Curriculum Framework 2024-2030 is replacing the 2015-2022 framework in phases (see the notes of the ZIMSEC chemistry and biology files). November 2026 and later O-Level candidates may be examined on a Heritage-Based Physics syllabus that could not be obtained. Confirm, add it as a new version file and give this version an effectiveTo.
The 'Experimental skills' node is ours, not a numbered topic: it holds the practical skills of syllabus objectives 4.1, 4.3 and 4.8 so practical-skills content can be tagged.
overview: The ZIMSEC O-Level Physics syllabus (Forms 3-4) covers fifteen topics: measurement, kinematics, forces, machines, mechanical structures, work, energy and power, thermal physics, internal combustion engines, waves, optics, electricity, magnetism, electromagnetism, electronics, and atomic and nuclear physics. It stresses understanding and applying physics to solve real problems, practical and ICT skills, safety and Zimbabwean contexts such as value addition in mining and industry.
assessmentOverview: Learners are assessed by continuous assessment and a national examination. The paper structure, durations and marks were not available in the source read and must be confirmed from the official syllabus or from ZIMSEC.

objectives.text: Measure length, area, volume, mass, time and temperature, reading instrument scales to the nearest fraction of a division (rulers, Vernier callipers, micrometer screw gauges, balances, stop-watches, thermometers, measuring cylinders).
Find the density of liquids and of regular and irregular solids by experiment, and relate density to floating and sinking.
Express quantities in SI units.
Derive units such as the newton, joule, watt and volt from the base units.
Define scalar and vector quantities and give examples of each.
Find the resultant of coplanar vectors by a graphical (scale drawing) method and apply it.

children.name: Speed, velocity and acceleration
children.description: Form 3: speed, velocity, distance, displacement and acceleration; equations of linear motion.

objectives.text: Define displacement, speed, velocity and acceleration.
Measure speed and acceleration with a ticker-tape timer or another method.
Use the equations of linear motion for constant acceleration to solve problems.
Plot, draw and interpret distance-time and speed-time graphs.
Find speed and acceleration from the slope of a graph and distance from the area under a speed-time graph.
Define free fall and determine the acceleration of free fall by experiment.
Describe qualitatively the motion of bodies falling in a uniform gravitational field, including terminal velocity.
Solve problems on motion under gravity.

children.name: Effect of force on shape and size of materials

objectives.text: Explain how a force changes the size and shape of a material, including tension and compression.
Plot, draw and interpret load-extension graphs.
Explain Hooke's law.
Calculate the spring constant.

children.name: Effect of force on motion
children.description: Form 3. Limited to linear motion; conservation of momentum is not required.

objectives.text: Define weight, momentum and inertia.
Calculate momentum using p = mv.
Explain each of Newton's three laws of motion.
Use the relationship F = ma between force, mass and acceleration.
Explain how friction affects the motion of a body, and state its advantages, disadvantages and ways of reducing it.
Describe the ways a force can change the motion of a body.
Describe qualitatively motion in a curved path caused by a force at right angles to the motion (centripetal force and acceleration).
Define the moment of a force.
Describe the moment of a force as its turning effect and give everyday examples.
Carry out an experiment to verify the principle of moments.
Calculate using the principle of moments.

children.name: Centre of mass
children.description: Form 3: centre of mass and centre of gravity.

objectives.text: Define centre of mass and centre of gravity.
Find the centre of mass of a plane lamina by experiment.
Describe qualitatively how the position of the centre of mass affects stability (stable, unstable and neutral equilibrium).

children.name: Pressure
children.description: Form 3: pressure in solids and fluids, atmospheric pressure and applications.

objectives.text: Define pressure and calculate it using p = F/A.
Calculate pressure in fluids using p = ρgh and describe how pressure changes with depth.
Describe atmospheric pressure and demonstrations of it.
Use pressure patterns to predict the type of weather, including wind strength and direction.
Describe the construction and use of a barometer and of a simple manometer.
Describe applications of fluid pressure such as hydraulic systems, pressure cookers and water reticulation.

children.name: Simple machines
children.description: Form 3. Levers, single-string pulley systems (at most six pulleys) and inclined planes; classification of levers is not required.

objectives.text: Describe the uses and applications of simple machines.
Calculate mechanical advantage, velocity ratio and efficiency.
Explain energy losses in machines.
Describe methods of improving efficiency.
Define a beam and describe beams by their cross-sectional shape.
Compare the strength of beams of different cross-sections and depths.
Explain the effects of push and pull forces on beams: compression, tension, shear and buckling.
Explain how stress is distributed in a loaded beam, including the neutral zone.
Construct trusses and explain the use of triangles in a truss.
Explain the advantages of trusses over beams.
Explain how a load is distributed through a truss.
Identify struts and ties in a truss.
Explain the design of a roof truss.
Describe methods of joining materials by pinning and by surface contact.
Compare the strengths of joints.
Identify materials used in large structures.
Compare the properties of construction materials: compressive and tensile strength, mass and durability.
Explain the design of, and materials used in, different types of bridge.
Explain the use of arches in large structures.
Explain the composition and shape of dam walls.
Define work done.
Calculate work done as force × distance.

children.name: Energy
children.description: Form 3: forms and sources of energy, conservation and conversions.

objectives.text: Define energy.
Describe forms and sources of energy, renewable and non-renewable.
Relate energy conversions to work done and apply the law of conservation of energy.
Calculate energy and work, including kinetic and gravitational potential energy.
Describe the safe disposal of batteries and accumulators.
Define power.
Relate power to the rate of energy transfer.
Calculate power, including P = Fv.

children.name: The kinetic theory of matter
children.description: Form 3: states of matter, Brownian motion, diffusion, Boyle's and Charles's laws and the equation of state.

objectives.text: Describe the states of matter and the effect of a change of state in terms of the kinetic theory.
Explain the physical properties of matter using the kinetic theory, including Brownian motion and diffusion.
Describe qualitatively the effect of temperature on the volume of a gas at constant pressure.
Use Boyle's law, Charles's law and the equation of state p1V1/T1 = p2V2/T2.

children.name: Thermal properties
children.description: Form 3: expansion, thermometers, melting and boiling, specific heat capacity, specific latent heat.

objectives.text: Compare qualitatively the expansion of solids, liquids and gases.
Explain applications and consequences of thermal expansion and contraction.
Describe how a physical property that varies with temperature is used to measure temperature, and name such properties.
State the need for fixed points and identify them; describe sensitivity, range and linearity.
Describe liquid-in-glass (laboratory and clinical) thermometers and thermocouples, with their advantages and disadvantages.
Define and describe melting and boiling as energy transfer without a change of temperature.
Describe the effect of impurities and pressure on melting and boiling points.
Determine the specific heat capacity of a liquid and a solid and calculate heat transfer from experimental data.
Explain why different materials have different heat capacities.
Define and calculate specific latent heat using Q = ml.
Identify good and bad conductors of heat and give a molecular account of conduction in solids.
Relate convection to density changes in liquids and gases.
Describe experiments to tell good and bad emitters and absorbers of infrared radiation apart, and deduce that good absorbers are good emitters.
Explain applications of conduction, convection and radiation, such as sea breezes and vacuum flasks.
Describe the function and design of a solar water heater.
Describe the operation of a four-stroke engine: inlet, compression, power and exhaust strokes.
Explain the role of the carburettor.
State the advantages of several cylinders in an engine.
Compare the operation of diesel and petrol engines.

children.name: Social and economic considerations of using fuels
children.description: Form 3. Numbered 8.1 again in the competency matrix; listed here as a second subtopic of topic 8.

objectives.text: Identify renewable and non-renewable fuels.
Describe the social and economic implications of using fuels, including deforestation and pollution.
Describe the safe handling of fuels.
Describe wave motion, transverse and longitudinal waves.
Describe amplitude, wavelength, frequency and period.
Calculate velocity, frequency and wavelength using v = fλ and T = 1/f.
Describe the propagation of waves using wavefronts and rays, including reflection and refraction.
Describe how sound is produced and the longitudinal nature of sound waves.
State the approximate range of audible frequencies.
Explain why sound needs a medium.
Describe experiments to find the speed of sound in air.
Relate pitch, loudness and quality to the amplitude and frequency of sound waves.
Describe echoes and their applications.

children.name: Electromagnetic waves
children.description: Form 3. No recall of actual wavelengths or frequencies is required.

objectives.text: Identify the regions of the electromagnetic spectrum in order of wavelength or frequency.
State the similarities and differences between electromagnetic waves.
State uses of the different regions of the electromagnetic spectrum.
Describe an experiment to illustrate the laws of reflection.
Use the law that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.
Describe the position and characteristics of the image formed by a plane mirror.
Carry out simple constructions, measurements and calculations for plane mirrors.
State the laws of refraction and describe refraction with ray diagrams.
Describe refraction of light through transparent blocks and liquids, including apparent depth.
Define refractive index.
Define the critical angle and describe total internal reflection.
Describe applications of total internal reflection such as optical fibres, prisms and mirages.

children.name: Lenses
children.description: Form 4. No treatment of images formed by diverging lenses; no magnification calculations.

objectives.text: Describe the action of converging and diverging lenses on a beam of light.
Draw ray diagrams to show the formation of real and virtual images by a converging lens.
Explain how to measure the focal length of a converging lens.
Describe magnification by a converging lens and the use of a single lens as a magnifying glass and to form a real image.
Explain the use of lenses to correct short and long sight.
Define and describe the dispersion of light by a glass prism, naming the colours in order.

children.name: Electrostatics
children.description: Form 4. Qualitative treatment of fields only.

objectives.text: Describe experiments to show electrostatic charging.
Describe the forces between charges.
Describe an electric field and simple field patterns with their direction.
Distinguish between electrical conductors and insulators.
Explain the separation of charge by induction.
Describe natural phenomena of static electricity, such as lightning, and the use of lightning conductors.
Use the idea that e.m.f. is measured by the energy a source gives in driving charge round a complete circuit.
Show that the volt is a joule per coulomb.
List sources of e.m.f., including primary, secondary and photovoltaic cells.
Explain the flow of current in a circuit and use I = Q/t.
Measure current and potential difference with ammeters and voltmeters.
Define potential difference and use the fact that the p.d.s in a series circuit add up to the total.
State and apply Ohm's law and state its limitations.
Describe an experiment to find resistance with a voltmeter and an ammeter.
Sketch and interpret V-I graphs for ohmic and non-ohmic conductors.
Use the relationship between resistance, length and cross-sectional area, R = ρl/A.
Set up simple electric circuits.
Draw and interpret circuit diagrams.
Use the fact that the current from the source is the sum of the branch currents in a parallel circuit.
Calculate the resistance of resistors in series and in parallel.
Describe uses of electricity in the home.
Calculate electrical power, energy and the cost of electricity using P = VI, E = VIt and the kilowatt-hour.
Describe electrical hazards and safety precautions.
Describe the wiring of a three-pin plug.
Explain the use of fuses, fuse ratings and switches in the live wire, and double insulation.
State the properties of magnets.
Describe magnetic field lines around magnets.
Explain induced magnetism.
Describe methods of magnetisation (stroking, using a solenoid) and demagnetisation (hammering, heating, electrical methods).
Distinguish between magnetic and non-magnetic materials and between the magnetic properties of iron and steel.
Describe uses of temporary magnets.
Describe uses and applications of permanent magnets.

children.name: Magnetic effect of an electric current

objectives.text: Describe an experiment to show that a current-carrying conductor has a magnetic field around it.
Describe an experiment to plot the field pattern of a current-carrying solenoid.
Predict the direction of the field around a straight conductor and a solenoid (right-hand grip rule).

children.name: Force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field

objectives.text: Describe an experiment to show that a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field experiences a force.
Describe the field patterns between parallel currents and relate them to the forces between the currents.
Predict the direction of motion of a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field (Fleming's left-hand rule).
Describe applications of the magnetic effect of a current, such as the electric bell and the relay.
Describe the operation of a d.c. motor.
Describe an experiment showing that a changing magnetic field can induce an e.m.f.
State the factors affecting the size of an induced e.m.f.
Use the fact that an induced e.m.f. opposes the change producing it (Lenz's law).
Predict the direction of an induced current (Fleming's right-hand rule).
Describe the operation of a.c. and d.c. generators and the differences between them.
Describe the structure and principle of operation of a basic iron-cored transformer.
Use the transformer equations Vp/Vs = Np/Ns and VpIp = VsIs.
Describe the use of transformers in high-voltage transmission.
Discuss energy losses in transformers and cables, including eddy currents and heating.
Give the advantages of high-voltage transmission.
Explain that a hot filament emits electrons.
Describe how these electrons are directed into a beam.
Describe the effect of a magnetic or electric field on an electron beam.
Describe the function of diodes and light-emitting diodes, including their circuit symbols.
Define rectification.
Explain half-wave and full-wave rectification with voltage-time graphs.
Describe resistor tolerance and use a colour code to find resistance values.
Choose components with suitable power ratings.
Describe the action of a variable potential divider.
Describe the action of thermistors and light-dependent resistors.
Describe the action of a capacitor.
Explain the use of reed switches in circuits.

children.name: Logic gates
children.description: Form 4. Listed in the scope and sequence chart (circuit symbols; construction of truth tables); its competency-matrix page could not be read, so its number and objectives are not confirmed.

objectives.text: Recognise the circuit symbols of logic gates and construct their truth tables.

children.name: Atomic model
children.description: Form 4: description of an atomic model; isotopes (from the scope and sequence chart).

objectives.text: Describe a model of the atom.
Explain what isotopes are.

children.name: Radioactivity
children.description: Form 4: definition; types of radioactive emission and their characteristics; use, storage, handling and impact of radioactive emissions (from the scope and sequence chart).

objectives.text: Define radioactivity.
Describe the types of radioactive emission and their characteristics.
Describe the uses, storage, handling and impact of radioactive emissions.

topics.name: Experimental skills
topics.description: Not a numbered topic: the practical and experimental skills of syllabus objectives 4.1, 4.3 and 4.8 (following instructions, measuring, recording and analysing data, safety), assessed in practical work.

objectives.text: Follow instructions in practical work to manipulate apparatus, record observations and analyse data to confirm or establish relationships.
Measure and express physical quantities in SI units to a suitable accuracy and precision.
Apply safety measures in all practical work.
